sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Telisotuzumab vedotin (Teliso-V) is a c-Met–directed antibody–drug conjugate comprising the monoclonal antibody telisotuzumab and the monomethyl auristatin E payload. Primary analysis of the phase 2 LUMINOSITY trial (NCT03539536) revealed Teliso-V monotherapy 1.9 mg/kg elicited durable responses and had generally manageable safety in patients with locally advanced or metastatic c-Met protein overexpressing, EGFR wild-type, nonsquamous NSCLC. We present updated outcomes with approximately 6 months longer follow-up and explore the impact of previous therapies.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Patients (≥18 y; had previous therapy including ≤1 chemotherapy) received 1.9 mg/kg Teliso-V every 2 weeks. c-Met protein overexpression (clinical trial assay for MET [SP44] [Roche]) was defined as greater than or equal to 25% tumor cells with 3+ staining intensity (c-Met high: ≥50% 3+; c-Met intermediate: 25 to <50% 3+). Primary end point was the overall response rate by independent central review per the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: As of February 21, 2024, 172 patients received at least one dose of Teliso-V; 168 patients (c-Met high, n = 84; c-Met intermediate, n = 84) were evaluable for efficacy. The overall response rate was 29.2% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 22.4–36.7; c-Met high, 34.5% [24.5–45.7]; c-Met intermediate, 23.8% [15.2–34.3]). Median duration of response was 7.2 months (95% CI: 5.5–11.0; c-Met high, 7.2 [95% CI: 4.2–12.0]; c-Met intermediate, 7.2 [95% CI: 4.7–11.5]). Previous therapy (platinum, immune checkpoint inhibitors, or both) did not impact efficacy outcomes. The most common treatment-related adverse event was peripheral sensory neuropathy (any-grade: 31%; grade ≥3: 7%).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Teliso-V monotherapy 1.9 mg/kg elicited durable responses, irrespective of the type of previous therapy received, and maintained a manageable safety profile in patients with c-Met protein overexpressing EGFR wild-type, nonsquamous NSCLC.
Keywords: c-Met protein, Biomarker, NSCLC, Telisotuzumab vedotin, Antibody–drug conjugate

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The receptor tyrosine kinase c-Met (also known as MET) protein is encoded by the MET protooncogene, and under physiologic functions, it plays a crucial role in cell proliferation, survival, and angiogenesis.1,2 MET is a recognized oncogenic driver in NSCLC and is often dysregulated, leading to tumorigenesis and resistance to therapy.1, 2, 3, 4, 5 Partially overlapping mechanisms of MET dysregulation include c-Met protein overexpression and MET gene alterations, such as exon 14 skipping mutations, amplification, and fusion.6 Separate from any role in acquired resistance to targeted therapies in oncogene-addicted NSCLC, primary c-Met dysregulation most typically occurs through protein overexpression, with approximately 24% of patients with nonsquamous EGFR wild-type NSCLC presenting c-Met protein overexpression.7 In addition to the higher prevalence, reports indicate that c-Met overexpression is a poor prognostic factor in NSCLC,3,8,9 which underscores the importance of this new biomarker. In a real-world study, patients with nonsquamous metastatic NSCLC and c-Met overexpression (defined as MET immunohistochemistry [IHC] positivity in at least 25% of tumor cells with 3+ intensity) had an unadjusted hazard ratio for death of 2.04 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.02–4.10) when compared with patients without c-Met overexpression.3 In another report, patients with high c-Met protein overexpression (≥50% tumor cells staining at 3+ intensity) had shortened survival (9.0 mo) compared with patients with c-Met low or no overexpression (18.0 mo) when examining overall survival (OS) from the start of first-line treatment, corroborating the negative prognostic value of c-Met protein overexpression.9 Telisotuzumab vedotin (Teliso-V) is the first approved therapy specifically for the c-Met protein overexpressing NSCLC population.

Teliso-V is a first-in-class c-Met protein–directed antibody–drug conjugate (ADC) comprising a humanized monoclonal antibody (telisotuzumab) conjugated to the cytotoxic microtubule inhibitor monomethyl auristatin E through a cleavable valine-citrulline linker. Teliso-V targets tumor cells by using c-Met protein expression as a biomarker to directly deliver its cytotoxic payload.10 The phase 2, two-stage LUMINOSITY trial was designed to identify the c-Met protein overexpressing NSCLC population best suited to treatment with Teliso-V in the second- or third-line setting and to further evaluate Teliso-V efficacy in the selected population. The nonsquamous EGFR wild-type NSCLC population met the protocol-specified criteria for expansion in stage 2. The primary analysis revealed durable responses and a generally manageable safety profile in this population.7 On the basis of the LUMINOSITY study (NCT03539536), the U.S. Food and Drug Administration granted accelerated approval to Teliso-V for the treatment of adult patients with locally advanced or metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC with high c-Met protein overexpression (≥50% 3+), as determined by a test approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, who had received a previous systemic therapy. Here, we present an updated analysis of efficacy and safety in patients with c-Met protein overexpressing, nonsquamous, EGFR wild-type NSCLC treated with Teliso-V 1.9 mg/kg in LUMINOSITY. This updated analysis provides approximately 6 months of follow-up compared with the previously reported results and explores the impact of previous therapies on clinical outcomes.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: The LUMINOSITY trial was a phase 2, multicenter, nonrandomized, two-stage study (NCT03539536) (Supplementary Fig. 1). Full study details have been published previously.7 In brief, three cohorts of patients stratified by histological type and EGFR mutation status were enrolled in stage 1, and, per protocol, stage 2 only enrolled the cohort(s) that met the predefined expansion criteria in stage 1. The nonsquamous EGFR wild-type cohort was expanded in stage 2. This publication reports on updated safety and efficacy in the cohort of patients with nonsquamous EGFR wild-type NSCLC enrolled in stages 1 and 2. Teliso-V was dosed at 1.9 mg/kg intravenously once every 2 weeks in stages 1 and 2. An additional cohort assessing a dose of 1.6 mg/kg once every 2 weeks was added; these results will be reported separately. Patients received Teliso-V until disease progression or study discontinuation criteria were met. Per protocol, toxicity management included dose interruptions of up to 42 days after the scheduled dosing date and dose reductions in increments of 0.3 mg/kg, down to a minimum dose of 1.0 mg/kg. The study was approved by regulatory and independent ethics committees/institutional review boards at each site and conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice Guidelines of the International Conference on Harmonization. All patients provided written informed consent before any study procedures were performed.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: The full eligibility criteria have been published previously.7 Briefly, eligible patients were 18 years and older with locally advanced or metastatic c-Met protein–overexpressing NSCLC. For the cohort presented in the current article, nonsquamous histological type and EGFR wild-type status were required. Patients with other actionable genomic alterations were eligible. Other key eligibility criteria included previous systemic therapy in the locally advanced or metastatic setting, including a maximum of one line of cytotoxic chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and, if eligible, therapy targeting driver gene alterations; an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1; and measurable disease per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 (RECIST v1.1).11 c-Met protein overexpression (clinical trial assay for MET [SP44] [Roche Diagnostics]) was defined as at least 25% of tumor cells with staining at 3+ intensity (c-Met high: ≥50% of tumor cells with 3+ intensity; c-Met intermediate: ≥25% to <50% of tumor cells with 3+ intensity) for patients with nonsquamous NSCLC. Key exclusion criteria were active brain metastases, history of interstitial lung disease (ILD) or pneumonitis that required treatment with systemic steroids, and history of ILD or pneumonitis within 3 months of the first dose.

sec.title: End Points and Assessments
sec.p: The primary end point was overall response rate (ORR) by independent central review (ICR), as assessed per RECIST v1.1.11 Secondary end points were duration of response (DOR), disease control rate (per RECIST v1.1), and progression-free survival (PFS), all per ICR, and OS. Tumor assessments through computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging were performed at baseline and then every 6 weeks for the first 12 months, every 8 weeks for the subsequent 12 months, and every 12 weeks thereafter.

Adverse events (AEs) were assessed after initial study drug administration and continued until 30 days after the final dose of Teliso-V. AEs were reported using Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) Preferred Terms and graded per National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 4.03. Investigator-reported suspected cases of ILD were reviewed and subsequently classified as ILD or non-ILD by an adjudication committee. Such cases included site-reported AEs of pneumonitis and ILD, and other related preferred terms. Peripheral neuropathy events and ILD events were also summarized on the basis of standardized MedDRA queries (SMQ; peripheral neuropathy SMQ narrow; ILD SMQ broad), and ocular surface disorders on the basis of corneal epitheliopathy per customized MedDRA query (Supplementary Table 1). Peripheral neuropathy, pneumonitis/ILD, and ocular surface disorders were monitored as AEs of special interest during the study.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: A detailed description of the statistical analysis of the LUMINOSITY trial has been previously published.7 All patients who received at least one dose of Teliso-V at 1.9 mg/kg every 2 weeks were included in the safety analyses. All dosed patients with c-Met protein overexpression were included in efficacy analyses.

The primary end point, ORR, was summarized together with two-sided 95% exact CI. Time-to-event end points were summarized by median time corresponding to the 50% event probability with two-sided 95% CIs estimated using the Brookmeyer and Crowley method.12 The 6-month PFS and 12-month OS were estimated using Kaplan–Meier methodology, along with 95% CI calculated with the SE derived from the Greenwood formula.13 Patients who had no postbaseline tumor assessment were defined as nonresponders (for ORR and DOR). For patients who were progression-free and alive, PFS was censored at the date of the last tumor assessment. For patients without any postbaseline tumor assessments who were alive at the data cutoff, PFS was censored at the day of the first dose. For patients with no reported death, OS was censored at the last date the patient was known to be alive.

sec.title: Patients and Treatment
sec.p: As of the data cutoff of February 21, 2024, 172 patients with nonsquamous EGFR wild-type NSCLC had received at least one dose of Teliso-V 1.9 mg/kg once every 2 weeks. The efficacy-evaluable population comprised 168 patients with c-Met protein overexpression, of whom 84 were c-Met high and 84 were c-Met intermediate. The median duration of follow-up was 24.9 months (95% CI: 19.4–26.6). The baseline demographics and disease characteristics are shown in Table 1. The median age was 64.5 years (range 33–83), and patients were predominantly male (69.6%), White (65.5%), and former tobacco users (62.5%). The median number of previous therapies was 1.0 (range 1.0–3.0), with 97.6% of patients having received previous platinum-based therapy, 80.4% having received previous immune checkpoint inhibitors, 78.6% having received platinum-based and immune checkpoint inhibitors, and 8.3% having received previous targeted therapies.

sec.p: At data cutoff, 167 patients (97.1%) had discontinued the study drug. The most common primary reason for study drug discontinuation was disease progression per RECIST v1.1 (50.6%). The median treatment duration was 4.5 months (range 0.03–28.8). In total, 130 patients (75.6%) discontinued the study; the most common reason was death (69.2%).

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: Efficacy data are summarized in Table 2. ORR per ICR was 34.5% (95% CI: 24.5–45.7) for the c-Met high, 23.8% (95% CI: 15.2–34.3) for the c-Met intermediate, and 29.2% (95% CI: 22.4–36.7) for the c-Met overexpressing total populations. A reduction in tumor size was observed in 75% (126/168) of patients (Fig. 1). Responses were durable, with median DOR of 7.2 months (95% CI: 4.2–12.0), 7.2 months (95% CI: 4.7–11.5), and 7.2 months (95% CI: 5.5–11.0) for the c-Met high, c-Met intermediate, and c-Met overexpressing total populations, respectively. Among responders, a DOR of at least 6 months was observed for 58.6% of patients with c-Met high, 45.0% with c-Met intermediate, and 53.1% for the c-Met overexpressing total population (Fig. 2). The median time to onset of response was 1.4 months (range 1.0–7.4) for the c-Met overexpressing total population. The median PFS per ICR was 5.5 months (95% CI: 4.1–6.8) for the c-Met high, 5.9 months (95% CI: 4.5–8.1) for the c-Met intermediate, and 5.6 months (95% CI: 4.6–6.8) for the c-Met overexpressing total populations (Supplementary Fig. 2A). The median OS was 14.3 months (95% CI: 9.0–25.4) for the c-Met high, 14.2 months (95% CI: 9.6–16.4) for the c-Met intermediate, and 14.2 months (95% CI: 9.9–16.4) for the c-Met overexpressing total populations (Supplementary Fig. 2B).

sec.p: The efficacy of Teliso-V was generally comparable in subgroups of patients who received previous platinum, previous immune checkpoint inhibitors, or previous platinum plus immune checkpoint inhibitors compared with the overall population (Table 3). Notably, 41.1% of patients received subsequent anticancer therapies, including 20.2% receiving microtubule inhibitors, with 14.9% having had docetaxel-based therapy.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Any-grade and grade 3 or higher (≥3) treatment-emergent AEs occurred in 167 patients (97.1%) and 98 (57.0%) patients, respectively. Treatment-related AEs (TRAEs) of any-grade occurred in 140 patients (81.4%); 49 patients (28.5%) experienced a grade ≥3 TRAE (Table 4). The most frequent any-grade TRAEs were peripheral sensory neuropathy (30.8%), peripheral edema (16.3%), and fatigue (14.0%); peripheral sensory neuropathy (7.0%), increased alanine aminotransferase (3.5%), and pneumonitis (2.9%) were the most common grade ≥3 events. TRAEs led to interruption in 53 patients (31.5%) and dose reduction in 45 patients (26.8%).

sec.p: Treatment-emergent AEs of special interest for Teliso-V included peripheral neuropathy, ocular surface disorders, and pneumonitis or ILD. These events are summarized in Supplementary Table 2. Peripheral neuropathy (SMQ narrow) events occurred in 43.6% of patients (treatment-related per investigator, 40.7%). Most events were mild or moderate, with 9.9% of patients presenting events grade ≥3 (treatment-related per investigator, 9.3%). The median time to onset of peripheral neuropathy was 101.0 (range 1–472) days (assessed by the investigator). Dose reductions because of peripheral neuropathy occurred in 18.0% of patients. Drug discontinuations because of peripheral neuropathy occurred in 11.6% of patients, with a median time to onset of the event that led to discontinuation of 238.5 days (range 57–519). In total, 24.4% of patients (treatment-related per investigator, 18.6%) experienced ocular surface disorders; the most frequent were blurred vision (12.2%), keratitis (6.4%), and dry eye (3.5%). Two (1.2%) patients presented grade ≥3 events (corneal opacity and blurred vision). The median time to onset of ocular surface disorders was 47.0 (range 1–319) days (assessed by the investigator). Dose reductions because of ocular surface disorders were observed in 2.9% of patients, and no ocular surface disorders led to treatment discontinuation. ILD events (SMQ broad) per investigator assessment occurred in 14% of patients. Most events were grade 1/2, with 3.5% of patients having grade ≥3 events. Per the adjudication committee, ILD events occurred in 9.9% of patients (grade ≥3: 5.2%; grade 5: 1.7%). Of the three grade 5 events, one death was considered related to ILD per the investigator (two were considered related to progressive disease per the investigator). More importantly, no additional ILD events occurred after the primary analysis. Treatment discontinuation because of ILD SMQ events occurred in 8.7% of patients, with a median time to event leading to discontinuation of 48.0 days (range 7–344). However, it should be noted that, per protocol, it was recommended that all patients who experienced ILD grade 2 or higher events should be discontinued from study treatment.

Although peripheral neuropathy was a typically reported event after treatment with Teliso-V, patients frequently received taxanes as subsequent anticancer therapy. Among patients without peripheral neuropathy SMQ events, 37.1% received one or more poststudy anticancer treatment, and 15.5% received poststudy taxanes. Among patients with peripheral neuropathy SMQ events, 45.3% had one or more poststudy anticancer treatment of any class, and 20% received poststudy taxanes.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this updated efficacy analysis of stage 2 of the LUMINOSITY trial, Teliso-V 1.9 mg/kg continued to exhibit durable responses in patients with c-Met protein overexpressing, nonsquamous, EGFR wild-type NSCLC. Patients with c-Met protein–overexpressing NSCLC have a markedly poor prognosis. Published data indicate shortened survival and a higher risk of death among patients with c-Met protein overexpression compared with those patients without.3,8,9 Teliso-V, a first-in-class c-Met–targeted ADC, is the first approved therapy of its kind to exhibit meaningful efficacy in this high-risk group, making the clinical benefit of Teliso-V particularly meaningful and offering a much-needed treatment option for patients in the second-line-and-beyond NSCLC setting.

This updated analysis evaluated ORR and DOR according to previous therapies. Nearly all patients enrolled received previous platinum, and most received both previous platinum and previous immune checkpoint inhibitory therapy. The results were consistent with the overall population, indicating that Teliso-V elicits durable responses in patients irrespective of the type of previous therapies. Moreover, a significant proportion of patients who discontinued Teliso-V were able to receive subsequent anticancer therapies, suggesting that patients remained fit for additional treatment after Teliso-V therapy.

Teliso-V maintained a manageable safety profile, with no new safety signals identified in this updated analysis. The toxicity profile was consistent with previous reports, with AEs of special interest also detailed in this publication (Supplementary Table 2). Peripheral neuropathy, despite being a common event among patients treated with Teliso-V and frequently associated with treatment discontinuation, had a median time to onset of events leading to discontinuation of nearly 8 months. This finding, besides corroborating the cumulative nature of this toxicity, suggests that patients were benefiting from treatment with Teliso-V, as they were able to remain on treatment for extended periods. Notably, patients who experienced peripheral neuropathy on study were still able to receive additional anticancer therapies, including agents associated with neuropathy. There was a numerically higher frequency of subsequent therapies, including taxanes, in patients who developed peripheral neuropathy SMQ events compared with those who did not develop peripheral neuropathy, indicating that patients have the opportunity to benefit not only from treatment with Teliso-V but also from subsequent therapies. Although ocular surface disorders were observed with Teliso-V treatment, these events were generally low grade (grade ≤2) and manageable with supportive care measures. Notably, no patients discontinued treatment because of ocular surface disorders. If ocular AEs occurred, referral to an eye care specialist was recommended for an ophthalmic examination and supportive treatment (e.g., lubricating or steroidal eye drops). ILD is a known risk with Teliso-V, typically occurring earlier in the course of treatment. Patients with grade 2 or higher events were advised to discontinue treatment, suggesting that early identification and proper management are key to reducing the risk of severe outcomes.

A key feature of the LUMINOSITY trial was the biomarker-guided patient selection, with a requirement for all enrolled patients to have c-Met protein–overexpressing NSCLC. This approach reflects the broader paradigm shift in oncology toward personalized, biomarker-driven therapeutics, which has been associated with increased clinical trial success rates compared with non–biomarker-selected approaches.14, 15, 16 Teliso-V represents one of the first ADCs to exhibit that biomarker overexpression by IHC in NSCLC directly correlates with clinical activity, allowing for better selection and optimized treatment outcomes with Teliso-V. Although c-Met overexpression and MET genomic alterations may coexist, they are not interchangeable. Although c-Met protein overexpression identified by IHC is observed in approximately 24% of patients with nonsquamous EGFR-wild-type NSCLC, MET amplification is observed in 5%, and MET exon 14 skipping mutation is observed in 2% to 4% of patients with NSCLC.7 It is important to note that reports indicate that most patients with c-Met overexpressing tumors do not exhibit MET amplification.3,17 Consequently, genomic profiling alone may fail to identify a substantial proportion of patients who could benefit from Teliso-V, highlighting the importance of proper biomarker testing. Of note, the prevalence of c-Met overexpression by IHC appears to be comparable whether assessed in archival (before the start of first-line) tumor samples or in postprogression samples (after progression on a previous line).18 As previously reported by Camidge et al.,7 over 90% of patients maintained the same or higher c-Met overexpression status in repeat biopsies compared with archival tissue in a paired sample analysis. These findings support the feasibility and clinical value of testing for c-Met overexpression early in the treatment course rather than delaying until disease progression.

With continued follow-up, the LUMINOSITY trial reaffirms that Teliso-V monotherapy 1.9 mg/kg delivers durable responses in patients with c-Met protein overexpressing, nonsquamous, EGFR wild-type NSCLC. The type of previous therapy was not a determinant of clinical outcomes. Given the poor prognosis and lack of effective treatment options for this population, the encouraging efficacy and manageable toxicity profile highlight Teliso-V as a valuable treatment option for patients with c-Met overexpression. These data support the potential use of Teliso-V monotherapy as second-line-and-beyond treatment in patients with c-Met protein overexpressing, nonsquamous, EGFR wild-type NSCLC. The ongoing global, randomized, phase 3 TeliMET NSCLC-01 trial (NCT04928846) is currently enrolling and is comparing Teliso-V vs docetaxel in this patient population.

sec.title: Data Sharing Statment
sec.p: AbbVie is committed to responsible data sharing regarding the clinical trials we sponsor. This includes access to anonymized, individual, and trial-level data (analysis data sets), and other information (eg, protocols, clinical study reports, synopses, or statistical analysis plans), as long as the trials are not part of an ongoing or planned regulatory submission.

These clinical trial data can be requested by any qualified researchers who engage in rigorous, independent, scientific research, and will be provided after review and approval of a research proposal, Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP), and execution of a Data Use Agreement (DUA). Data requests can be submitted at any time after approval in the US and Europe and after acceptance of this manuscript for publication. The data will be accessible for 12 months, with possible extensions considered. For more information on the process or to submit a request, visit the following link: https://vivli.org/ourmember/abbvie/ then select “Home.”
